text: It may be objected that the chapter merely follows the economy of ancient narrative, which seldom reports what its characters feel and never explains it; and the objection is in part just. But the narrator is not everywhere so silent. The reticence of this chapter is deliberate, and the narrator knows what he is about. In his voice restraint becomes a kind of accusation, for in other places he reports plainly what men feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps.
